questions.question: Which statement best describes FNP-level type 2 diabetes management?
choices: It is individualized cardiovascular, kidney, metabolic, and safety care—not A1c lowering alone
It is only about avoiding dietary carbohydrate
It can ignore medication access if A1c is elevated
It never requires screening for complications
questions.explanation: Diabetes care integrates glycemia, hypoglycemia prevention, cardiovascular and kidney risk, weight, foot and eye health, access, mental health, and patient-defined goals.

questions.question: A patient with diabetes has vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid deep breathing, severe weakness, and marked hyperglycemia. What is the priority?
choices: Urgent evaluation for a possible metabolic emergency
Wait for the next routine A1c
Increase exercise and reassess next month
Treat the message as a routine refill request
questions.explanation: Systemic symptoms with marked hyperglycemia can indicate ketoacidosis, hyperosmolar illness, dehydration, or another serious condition and require urgent assessment.

questions.question: Which factor should shape an individualized glycemic goal?
choices: Hypoglycemia risk, comorbidity, function, treatment burden, and patient priorities
Only the patient’s age
Only the most recent fasting glucose
A universal target applied to everyone
questions.explanation: Goals should balance expected benefit with risk, comorbidity, frailty, life expectancy, ability to self-manage, and what matters to the patient.

questions.question: Why might A1c not fully represent a patient's current glycemic exposure?
choices: Conditions affecting red-cell turnover, anemia, kidney disease, or transfusion can affect its interpretation
A1c always shows every low-glucose event
A1c replaces symptom assessment
A1c makes glucose monitoring unnecessary for every patient
questions.explanation: A1c is valuable but can be misleading in some clinical settings and does not show glucose variability or all hypoglycemic episodes.

questions.question: Which scenario increases risk for hypoglycemia?
choices: Insulin or secretagogue use with missed meals and declining kidney function
Stable food access with no glucose-lowering medication
A normal blood-pressure reading
Receiving a foot examination
questions.explanation: Insulin and secretagogues can cause hypoglycemia, especially with reduced intake, alcohol, dosing errors, increased activity, or declining renal function.

questions.question: A patient with type 2 diabetes and CKD has an acceptable A1c. Why may medication review still be needed?
choices: Some therapies may be selected for demonstrated cardiovascular and kidney benefit independent of A1c alone
A1c eliminates all kidney-risk assessment
All diabetes medications are unsafe in CKD
No treatment can affect cardiovascular risk
questions.explanation: For appropriate patients, modern diabetes therapy considers cardiorenal benefit as well as glucose lowering. Selection still requires individualized renal, safety, access, and guideline review.

questions.question: What is the safest response before intensifying therapy for unexpectedly high glucose readings?
choices: Review use, dose, injection or device technique, access, illness, diet change, and medication contributors
Assume the patient is nonadherent and double every dose
Ignore symptoms if A1c is old
Stop all treatment
questions.explanation: Unexpected hyperglycemia may reflect illness, technique, device error, access, medication effects, or disease progression. A focused assessment prevents unsafe reflexive changes.

questions.question: Which foot finding requires prompt escalation rather than routine annual follow-up?
choices: New ulcer with spreading redness or ischemic color change
Clean intact skin with no symptoms
A patient wearing comfortable shoes
A normal glucose-meter battery
questions.explanation: Ulceration, infection, ischemic change, systemic illness, or rapidly progressive neuropathic symptoms can threaten limb or life and need timely evaluation.

questions.question: What does teach-back contribute to diabetes care?
choices: It verifies that the patient can use the device, explain the plan, and respond to abnormal results
It replaces medication reconciliation
It is only useful for people using insulin
It makes follow-up unnecessary
questions.explanation: Teach-back detects misunderstandings about glucose monitoring, injections, medications, sick-day safety, and escalation. It is a safety intervention for any complex plan.

questions.question: Which describes a complete diabetes screening loop?
choices: Order indicated kidney, eye, foot, and cardiovascular assessments; review results; communicate findings; and arrange follow-up
Place referrals without tracking them
Perform only an A1c test indefinitely
Wait for symptoms before assessing complications
questions.explanation: Screening prevents disability only when results are reviewed, acted on, communicated, and followed through—not merely ordered.
